The slender rockfish (Scorpaena elongata) is a poorly-known scorpaenid inhabiting the continental shelf and upper slope of the western Mediterranean and adjacent Atlantic waters. Field surveys indicate that females attain sexual maturity upon reaching a total length of 32.5 cm [Lp = 32.5 cm], a size typically associated with the onset of gonadal recrudescence and vitellogenesis in this iteroparous teleost. Individuals reach a maximum recorded total length of 50 cm [Li = 50 cm], a value consistent with asymptotic body size estimates derived from mark-recapture studies conducted in the Alboran Sea. For females, the total length at puberty represents roughly sixty-five percent of the ultimate length, a ratio that aligns with life-history patterns observed in other demersal scorpaenids that exhibit moderate longevity and relatively late maturation. Growth increments slow considerably after sexual maturation, with energy increasingly directed toward reproductive effort rather than somatic expansion. The species is considered data-limited for stock assessment purposes, and these length-based metrics provide critical reference points for evaluating population status under a length-based harvest management framework for Mediterranean fisheries.

At a water temperature of 13.9 °C [T = 13.9 °C], a stable thermal regime characteristic of its deeper continental-shelf habitat, newly hatched larvae emerge from the egg after an incubation period of 15 days [ab = 15 days]. This comparatively short embryonic duration reflects the elevated metabolic rates sustained at this temperature and is typical of autumn-spawning scorpaenids whose eggs develop under moderately cool conditions prior to the winter mixing period. The hatchlings begin as yolk-sac larvae, with the mouth remaining closed during the first few days following eclosion by means of chorionase-mediated rupture of the chorion. The yolk reserves sustain the prolarvae during the initial endotrophic phase until the retinal differentiation and mouth gape opening permit the onset of exogenous feeding. The synchrony of hatching with the seasonal abundance of small copepod nauplii suggests that the timing of spawning is tightly coupled to prey availability during the early larval period, a critical window for survival in marine teleosts.

The wet weight at birth, representing the mass of a recently hatched yolk-sac larva, has been estimated at 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams] based on the relationship between egg diameter and larval mass derived from the congener Scorpaenichthys marmoratus. This initial mass is extraordinarily low, reflecting the small size of the pelagic, transparent eggs typical of broadcast-spawning scorpaenids. After the yolk-sac larva transitions to the exotrophically feeding stage, a period of rapid mass gain ensues, driven by the consumption of planktonic prey in the upper water column. The species' ultimate wet weight, or asymptotic adult body mass, reaches approximately 1500 grams [Wwi = approximately 1500 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship fitted to specimens collected across the species' geographic range. The contrast between the minuscule larval mass and the substantial adult mass underscores the extreme ontogenetic niche shift that occurs during the pelagic-benthic transition, with post-settlement juveniles experiencing a dramatic increase in available prey size and habitat complexity.

Reproductive output in Scorpaena elongata has been characterized through histological examination of ovaries from gravid individuals collected during the spawning season. At the same ambient water temperature of 13.9 °C [T = 13.9 °C], each mature female produces a batch of approximately 90 eggs per daily spawning event [Ri = approximately 90 eggs per daily spawning event], and the capacity to spawn daily results in 365 spawning events per year [F_R_i = 365 spawning events per year]. This high-frequency, low-volume reproductive strategy yields a substantial annual output, with females investing in repeated small batches of eggs rather than a single large clutch. The protracted vitellogenic period required to mature each batch of oocytes likely constrains the number of oocytes per event, a pattern shared with other deep-dwelling scorpaenids that experience relatively stable thermal and trophic conditions throughout the year. The reproductive cycle appears to be synchronized with the seasonal availability of zooplanktonic prey for the planktonic larvae, ensuring that the point of no return is avoided during the critical transition to exogenous feeding.

The maximum lifespan of the slender rockfish, a member of the family Scorpaenidae (order Scorpaeniformes), has been estimated at approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years] based on otolith increment counts from individuals captured in the Gulf of Lions at 13.9 °C [T = 13.9 °C]. This substantial longevity is characteristic of the Scorpaenidae, a family of relatively slow-growing, late-maturing fishes adapted to stable, resource-limited environments where predation risk on adults is low and reproductive value remains high into advanced age. The oldest individuals often exceed 40 cm in total length and exhibit strongly ossified fin rays, a reliable external indicator of advanced age in this genus. The combination of delayed female maturation at 32.5 cm [Lp = 32.5 cm], a thirty-year lifespan, and a high-frequency daily spawning strategy defines a conservative life-history strategy that renders the species particularly vulnerable to overexploitation by demersal trawl fisheries. The otolith-derived age data, cross-validated with length-frequency analysis, provide the foundation for age-structured population models used in regional fisheries assessments.
